setup.zh: 二试，脑子：一面石壁，刻着九个空格，一堆刻了数的石块。「横竖斜，加起来都要一样。」
setup.en: Second trial, wits: a stone wall carved with nine empty squares, a heap of numbered stones. "Across, down, corner to corner — they all add up the same."

recap.zh: 二试，洛书九宫：你想起娘教的口诀，「五居中央」。
recap.en: Second trial, the Luo Shu square: you remembered Mother's rhyme — "five in the middle."

en: A stone wall, nine empty squares.
"Across, down, corner to corner — all the same."

story.zh:
**二试 · 脑子。**

一试下来，站在石阶顶上的，不过四五百人。

二试是在山门里头的一片石坪上考的。石坪上立着几十面石壁，每面石壁上刻着九个空格，横三竖三，像一张棋盘，石壁底下堆着九块石头，每块石头上刻一个数，从一到九。一个管二试的老执事，背着手在石壁前走来走去，道：「横着加，竖着加，斜着加，都要一样。一炷香。」

四五百个孩子便围着石壁，抓耳挠腮。

有人把石头摆成了一朵花，有人把石头摞成了一座塔，有人两块两块地换来换去，换了半炷香，越换越乱，把自己换哭了。还有一个孩子，盯着那九块石头看了很久很久，然后把它们一块一块，全都塞进了嘴里。

那管二试的老执事走过来，叹了口气，在那孩子背上一拍，「噗噗噗」，九块石头一块一块吐了出来，吐在地下，排成歪歪扭扭的一行。老执事对旁边的执事道：「每三年都有一个。」旁边那执事道：「今年这个塞得多，上一回那个只塞了五块。」老执事点点头，道：「一届比一届饿。」

那孩子当时心里在想什么，沈小满到老也没想明白。

小满看着自己面前那九个格子，一时也发了懵。

他先是一个一个地试。一放在左上，九放在右下，中间放个五，横着一加，不对；换一换，又不对。铜炉里那炷香，一截一截地往下短，香灰落在炉沿上，落一截，他心里便紧一分。旁边那面石壁前的孩子，已经换哭了第二个。

他停住了手，心想：这么试下去，试到明年也试不完。九块石头，能摆出多少样来？他算不过来。算不过来的账，就别硬算，他娘说的。他识字，是他娘在油灯底下一个一个教的；他会算账，是他娘拿算盘珠子一颗一颗拨给他看的。可这九个格子，他娘没教过——

不。

他娘教过。

那是去年冬天的一个晚上，油灯底下，他娘教他打算盘，教烦了，便教他一个口诀，说是算账的人闲下来，拿来醒脑子的。他娘说，这口诀是她爹教她的；她爹，是一个教了一辈子蒙学、穷了一辈子的塾师，从一本旧书上看来的。至于是什么书，她爹没说，她也没问。那口诀是这么念的：

「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」

小满闭上眼睛，在心里念了一遍，一个字也没有差。
story.en:
**Second trial · Head.**

After the first trial, those standing at the top of the stair were no more than four or five hundred.

The second trial was held on a stone terrace inside the gate. On the terrace stood dozens of stone walls, each carved with nine empty squares, three across and three down, like a game board; at the foot of each lay nine stones, each carved with a number from one to nine. An old steward in charge of the second trial paced before the walls, hands behind his back. "Across, down, slantwise — all must add the same. One stick of incense."

So four or five hundred children crowded round the walls, scratching their heads.

Some arranged the stones into a flower; some stacked them into a pagoda; some swapped them two at a time, swapped half a stick of incense, the more they swapped the worse it got, and swapped themselves to tears. And one child stared at the nine stones a long, long time, then put them one by one, all of them, in his mouth.

The old steward came over, sighed, and slapped the child on the back — *pff, pff, pff* — and the nine stones came out one by one onto the ground in a crooked row. The old steward said to the steward beside him, "There's one every three years." The other said, "This year's stuffed more in. Last time it was only five." The old steward nodded. "Each lot hungrier than the last."

What that child was thinking at the time, Shen Xiaoman never did work out, even when he was old.

Xiaoman, looking at the nine squares in front of him, went blank for a moment too.

First he tried one by one. One top left, nine bottom right, five in the middle; add across — wrong; swap — wrong again. The incense in the bronze burner grew shorter segment by segment, the ash dropping onto the rim; each segment that dropped, his heart tightened. At the wall beside him a second child had swapped himself to tears.

He stopped and thought: try like this and I'll still be trying next year. Nine stones — how many ways can they go? More than he could count. A sum you can't work out, don't force it — his mother said so. He could read because his mother taught him character by character under the oil lamp; he could keep accounts because his mother flicked the abacus beads for him one by one. But these nine squares, his mother had never taught him —

No.

His mother had.

It was one evening last winter, under the oil lamp; teaching him the abacus, she'd tired of it and taught him a rhyme instead, one people who keep accounts use to clear their heads when idle. His mother said her father taught it to her; her father, a village tutor who taught children all his life and was poor all his life, had read it in an old book. What book, her father never said, and she never asked. The rhyme went like this:

"Wear nine, tread one; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four for shoulders, six and eight for feet; five in the middle."

Xiaoman shut his eyes and said it through in his head, not one word out.

exits.means: hands in the solved square, or asks to go on to the third trial

refuse.zh: 九宫还没填满。瞿老不看半张卷子。

story.zh:
五居中央。他便把刻着「五」的那块石头，放在了正中间。

头顶上戴着九，脚底下踩着一。左手三，右手七。两个肩膀是二和四，两只脚是六和八。他一块一块地摆，摆完了，横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，还是十五。

他站起身来，退后两步，看着那面石壁，看了很久。石壁上那九块石头，排得端端正正，倒像一个人，头戴着九，脚踩着一，张着两只胳膊，稳稳地站在那里。小满心想，原来是这样一个人。这个人他娘认得，他外公认得，他外公那本旧书认得，他从前不认得，今天认得了。

石坪外头，一道矮墙后面，马家的两个家丁正踮着脚，隔着墙冲马小宝打手势。一个伸出五根手指，拍拍自己的肚子；一个伸出九根手指——他两只手一共十根指头，伸出九根，便有一根弯着，弯得十分用力——拍拍自己的脑门。马小宝蹲在石壁底下，一面嚼桂花糕，一面照着比划摆石头。摆完了，横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，十四。

那管二试的老执事踱过去，看了看，又看了看墙头上那两颗还在比划的脑袋。两颗脑袋一下子缩了回去。老执事没有说话，在竹牌上画了一道——画的是什么，谁也没看见——背着手走了。

小满道：「我娘。」

老执事「嗯」了一声，又道：「知道这是什么么？」

小满摇头。

老执事也不管他听不听，自顾自地道：「这叫洛书。」

他在石壁跟前的一块石头上坐了下来，捶着腰，慢吞吞地讲。他说，上古的时候，天下发大水，一连发了许多年，山给淹了，地给淹了，人住在树上，跟鸟抢窝。有个叫鲧的，拿土去堵，堵了九年，没堵住，给杀了。鲧的儿子叫禹，接着治。禹不堵，他疏，哪里低，便把水往哪里引，引进河里，引进海里。他在外头治了十三年的水，三回路过自己家门口，一回也没有进去。

「后来洛水里爬上来一只大乌龟，背上驮着这九个数——这故事，你娘大约讲过。」老执事道，「禹照着它，把天下分成了九州，又收了九州的铜，铸了九口鼎，一州一口。」说到这里，他顿了一顿，朝身后那座山看了一眼，声音低了些，「这都是老辈子的话了。你娘教得好。」

说完，他在竹牌上画了一道，背着手走了。

小满站在那里，把「九口鼎」三个字在嘴里嚼了一遍。他想起吴婆婆说的，鼎是一口大锅。九口大锅，一州一口，那得煮多少饭。他觉得胸口那块木牌好像动了一下，伸手去摸，却是凉的。大约是自己心跳得快了，他想。

他转过身，石坪那一头，另一面石壁前，早有人摆好了。一个红鼻头的姑娘，蹲在石壁底下，拿一根炭条，在一个巴掌大的小本子上，低着头记着什么，记得十分专心。

小满瞧见那小本子，不由得一愣。这年头，谁出门考仙门，还随身带个本子记账？

他往那边走了两步，想瞧个仔细。人群一挤，一个胖孩子挤到他跟前，问他借的石头还不还，小满说我没借你石头，胖孩子说那就是别人借的，你帮我看看是谁。等小满把胖孩子打发走了，再抬头看时，那石壁底下已经空了，只地上留着一截用秃了的炭条头。
story.en:
Five in the middle. So he set the stone carved "five" right in the centre.

Nine worn on the head, one trodden underfoot. Three on the left hand, seven on the right. The shoulders two and four, the feet six and eight. He set them one by one, and when he'd done, added across: fifteen; down: fifteen; slantwise: still fifteen.

He stood up, stepped back two paces, and looked at the wall a long time. The nine stones stood there square and proper, like a person — nine on the head, one underfoot, arms spread, standing firm. Xiaoman thought: so that's who it is. His mother knew this person, his grandfather knew him, his grandfather's old book knew him; he hadn't before, and today he did.

Outside the terrace, behind a low wall, the Mas' two servants were on tiptoe signalling to Ma Xiaobao over it. One held up five fingers and patted his belly; one held up nine fingers — ten fingers on two hands, so one stayed bent, bent very hard — and patted his forehead. Ma Xiaobao crouched at his wall, eating osmanthus cake, setting the stones by the signals. Done, he added across: fifteen; down: fifteen; slantwise: fourteen.

The old steward strolled over, looked, then looked at the two heads on top of the wall still signalling. The two heads shrank back at once. The old steward said nothing, drew a stroke on his bamboo tally — what stroke, nobody saw — and walked off with his hands behind his back.

The old steward strolled over, hands behind his back, looked at the wall Xiaoman had set, then at him. "Who taught you?"

Xiaoman said, "My mother."

The old steward said "Mm," and then: "Know what this is?"

Xiaoman shook his head.

The old steward, whether he was listening or not, said: "This is called the Luo Writing."

He sat down on a stone before the wall, thumping his back, and talked slowly. In high antiquity, he said, the world flooded, flooded year after year; mountains drowned, land drowned, people lived in trees and fought the birds for nests. A man called Gun tried to stop it with earth; he stopped it nine years, didn't manage, and was killed. Gun's son was called Yu, and took up the taming. Yu didn't block; he channelled — wherever was low, he led the water there, into rivers, into the sea. He tamed the waters thirteen years out there, passed his own door three times, and not once went in. "Later a great tortoise climbed out of the Luo with these nine numbers on its back — your mother has probably told you that one," the old steward said. "By it Yu divided the world into the Nine Provinces, gathered the Nine Provinces' bronze, and cast nine *ding*, one to a province." Here he paused, glanced back at the mountain behind him, and lowered his voice. "All old sayings now. Your mother taught you well."

Done, he drew a stroke on his bamboo tally and walked off with his hands behind his back.

Xiaoman stood there and chewed the words *nine ding* over once. He remembered Granny Wu saying a *ding* is a big pot. Nine big pots, one to a province — how much rice would that cook. He felt the token at his chest seem to move; he reached for it, but it was cool. His heart beating fast, probably, he thought.

He turned. At the far end of the terrace, before another wall, someone had already finished. A red-nosed girl crouched at the foot of the wall with a stick of charcoal, head down, writing something in a palm-sized notebook, very intently.

Seeing the notebook, Xiaoman stopped short. Who goes to sit the immortal gate these days carrying a notebook for accounts?

He took two steps that way for a closer look. The crowd shifted, a fat child pushed up in front of him asking if he'd give back the stones he'd borrowed; Xiaoman said he hadn't borrowed any; the fat child said then someone else had, would he help him find out who. By the time Xiaoman had got rid of the fat child and looked up again, the foot of the wall was empty; on the ground lay only a worn-down stub of charcoal.
